extracted.intended_audience: novelists and fiction writers preparing submission materials or deciding whether a manuscript is ready to pitch (agents/editors as implicit evaluators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for evaluating a novel/memoir opening (first ~50 pages) to determine whether the manuscript is ready to pitch to agents or editors. Focuses on pitch materials alignment and narrative elements that industry pros look for in the opening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synopsis clarity / reveals story weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the synopsis first because 'when it doesn't quite make sense, that's a good indication that there are issues with the plot and/or character arc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear, coherent synopsis should show a through line and an escalating central source of conflict. If the synopsis indicates no central conflict, disconnected storylines, or no real climax/transformative turning point, those are red flags that the manuscript needs structural work before pitching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query letter + synopsis alignment (pitch materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: A compelling query letter plus a synopsis that makes sense can get an agent or editor's attention; the opening must match the book described in your pitch materials ('Does this opening sound like the opening of the book described in your pitch materials?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the first pages deliver the premise promised in the query/synopsis. If the pitch promises certain elements or stakes, the opening should reflect that promise or the submission risks disappointing readers/market gatekeepers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear point-of-view / whose head we're in
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it clear whose head we're in within the first few paragraphs?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous or shifting head-space in the opening confuses readers and agents; establish POV quickly so the reader can orient to the protagonist and narrative perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of stakes (it matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a sense that there's something real at stake in this story, that it matters?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openings should convey consequences or risk so readers care about outcomes. Lack of palpable stakes undermines reader engagement and reduces the likelihood of an agent requesting the full manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelling voice and clear prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the voice compelling, the prose clear?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voice and clarity are basic gatekeeping criteria; strong, distinct voice and lucid prose in the first pages signal craft and make an agent more likely to read on. Poorly expressed voice or muddy prose are immediate negatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition and backstory balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there enough exposition for the reader to make sense of what's happening and to understand where the protagonist is coming from? 'Less is more' often applies, but withholding too much information for too long prevents hooking the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient worldbuilding and protagonist backstory early enough to orient readers without heavy-handed info-dumps. The anti-pattern is withholding essential context so long that readers can't follow or invest in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise of the premise (deliver early)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the opening deliver on the premise promised in the synopsis/query? Example given: if premise involves a unicorn, the unicorn shouldn't first appear on page 40.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't delay the core premise element(s) so long that the submission fails to fulfill its own promise. If the central hook of the pitch doesn't appear early enough, the manuscript may be considered as 'starting in the wrong place.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing: inciting incident and early plot development by page 50
rubrics_metrics.description: By page 50 there should usually be the inciting incident and at least one more major plot development; absence suggests pacing is off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong openings typically include an inciting incident and additional plot movement within ~50 pages. A manuscript that shows a compelling development by page 50 often indicates the author has an intuitive command of pacing and is more likely to get a full request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative tension (questions/conflict that propel reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there narrative tension — arising from conflict or from questions the story raises — that keeps the reader turning the pages?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tension can be interpersonal (e.g., falling out), global (e.g., impending war), or question-based (e.g., who killed the jogger?). The presence of such tension at the end of a 50-page sample is a major factor prompting agents/editors to request the full manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorter submission criteria (20 pages or less)
rubrics_metrics.description: For shorter requested samples: agents look for clarity and command of craft; voice; a character readers can root for; and a sense that the story has real stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When submitting only 20 pages or less, prioritize demonstrating craft, distinct voice, and compelling character/stakes early, since you have less space to develop inciting incidents or longer arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-editing / readiness check process
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare your query letter and synopsis, put both them and your manuscript aside for a few days or weeks, then read them as if you were a publishing pro to determine readiness to pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give yourself distance before evaluating; compare opening to pitch materials and assess voice, pacing, and tension freshly. Also recommended: volunteer as a reader for a literary journal or small press to learn to evaluate openings the way industry pros do.
